title: How to prompt ChatGPT like an intern manager: few-shot, chain-of-thought, and EasyGen's LinkedIn growth
summary: Ruben explains why generic ChatGPT prompts give generic output: LLMs are next-word predictors, so you must supply examples (few-shot) and steps (chain-of-thought) and treat the model like a precise but literal intern. He also covers using AI for brainstorming volume rather than education, and how EasyGen helped two employees hit 1M LinkedIn views in 25 days.

principles.text: Zero-shot prompts produce generic output; give examples (few-shot) of your own best work first.
principles.quote: Zero-shot means that you give it zero example before you get the results, okay? But few-shot prompting means that you give multiple examples before you get the output.

principles.text: LLMs are glorified next-word predictors, so default output is generic by design; prompt for the twist you want.
principles.quote: It's going to be as generic as possible, as dull as possible. But but it's not even a problem. It is trained that way. It is meant to be that way.

principles.text: Use chain-of-thought: spell out the steps you would take and have the AI wait for your approval between them.
principles.quote: So, you are the one doing the steps. It's called chain-of-thoughts.

principles.text: Treat the LLM as a tireless but literal intern; anything you think is obvious must be stated.
principles.quote: everything that you think is obvious is not to an intern. It's totally not to an LLM.

principles.text: Use AI to generate a thousand options, then you select the best; it is not a one-button perfect answer.
principles.quote: No, you press one button and you get a thousand solutions and then you select the best one.

principles.text: Make content about the audience going from A to B, not about you.
principles.quote: It's not about me when I'm making a post. It's about you who's listening. I need to help you go from A to B.
